evidence.title: An HPC-Based Hydrothermal Finite Element Simulator for Modeling Underground Response to Community-Scale Geothermal Energy Production
evidence.abstract: Geothermal heat, as renewable energy, shows great advantage with respect to its environmental impact due to its significantly lower CO2 emissions than conventional fossil fuel. Open and closed-loop geothermal heat pumps, which utilize shallow geothermal systems, are an efficient technology for cooling and heating buildings, especially in urban areas. Integrated use of geothermal energy technologies for district heating, cooling, and thermal energy storage can be applied to optimize the subsurface for communities to provide them with multiple sustainable energy and community resilience benefits. The utilization of the subsurface resources may lead to a variation in the underground environment, which might further impact local environmental conditions. However, very few simulators can handle such a highly complex set of coupled computations on a regional or city scale. We have developed high-performance computing (HPC) based hydrothermal finite element (FE) simulator that can simulate the subsurface and its hydrothermal conditions at a scale of tens of km. The HPC simulator enables us to investigate the subsurface thermal and hydrologic response to the built underground environment (such as basements and subways) at the community scale. In this study, a coupled hydrothermal simulator is developed based on the open-source finite element library deal.II. The HPC simulator was validated by comparing the results of a benchmark case study against COMSOL Multiphysics, in which Aquifer Thermal Energy Storage (ATES) is modeled and a process of heat injection into ATES is simulated. The use of an energy pile system at the Treasure Island redevelopment site (San Francisco, CA, USA) was selected as a case study to demonstrate the HPC capability of the developed simulator. The simulator is capable of modeling multiple city-scale geothermal scenarios in a reasonable amount of time.

evidence.title: Optimization of Closed-Loop Shallow Geothermal Systems Using Analytical Models
evidence.abstract: Closed-loop shallow geothermal systems are one of the key technologies for decarbonizing the residential heating and cooling sector. The primary type of these systems involves vertical borehole heat exchangers (BHEs). During the planning phase, it is essential to find the optimal design for these systems, including the depth and spatial arrangement of the BHEs. In this work, we have developed a novel approach to find the optimal design of BHE fields, taking into account constraints such as temperature limits of the heat carrier fluid. These limits correspond to the regulatory practices applied during the planning phase. The approach uses a finite line source model to simulate temperature changes in the ground in combination with an analytical model of heat transport within the boreholes. Our approach is demonstrated using realistic scenarios and is expected to improve current practice in the planning and design of BHE systems.

evidence.title: On the Size of Minimal Separators for Treedepth Decomposition
evidence.abstract: Treedepth decomposition has several practical applications and can be used to speed up many parameterized algorithms. There are several works aiming to design a scalable algorithm to compute exact treedepth decompositions. Those include works based on a set of all minimal separators. In those algorithms, although a number of minimal separators are enumerated, the minimal separators that are used for an optimal solution are empirically very small. Therefore, analyzing the upper bound on the size of minimal separators is an important problem because it has the potential to significantly reduce the computation time. A minimal separator $S$ is called an optimal top separator if $td(G) = |S| + td(G \backslash S)$, where $td(G)$ denotes the treedepth of $G$. Then, we have two theoretical results on the size of optimal top separators. (1) For any $G$, there is an optimal top separator $S$ such that $|S| \le 2tw(G)$, where $tw(G)$ is the treewidth of $G$. (2) For any $c < 2$, there exists a graph $G$ such that any optimal top separator $S$ of $G$ have $|S| > c \cdot tw(G)$, i.e., the first result gives a tight bound on the size of an optimal top separator.

evidence.title: Oil/water separation in a novel cyclone separator
evidence.abstract:
Conventional bulk oil-water separation is performed in large gravity separators that take
up large areas and potentially contain large volumes of hazardous material. An
intensified bulk separator has the potential to provide significant benefit in saving space,
especially where this is at a premium, and in improving safety.
The I-SEP, a novel geometry of Axial-Flow Cyclone (also known as Uniflow or
straight-through) separator, has been tested as an intensified bulk oil-water separator.
The objective of this work is to quantify performance by producing a map of separation
performance with variation of inlet conditions, using variation of outlet back pressure to
make the separator adaptable to variable inlet flow. A second objective is to compare
the experimental performance of the I-SEP with a mathematical model.
Using a Perspex test-unit with kerosene, or a silicone-based oil, and water in a batch
flow loop, a map has been produced for outlet compositions and separation efficiencies
at multiple inlet velocities. This was done for a range of inlet water cuts from 10% to
90% and with a geometry varied by lengthening the separating chamber of the test unit.
A Computational Fluid Dynamics model using the Reynolds-Stress model has been
developed with the FLUENT 6.0 CFD code. This has been compared with quantitative
flow visualisation data and drop sizing information to model the separation of the
cyclone by a discrete-phase technique.
An optimum configuration and operating conditions has been found, with peak
efficiencies in excess of 80%. This shows the important effect in improving
performance achieved by the manipulation of outlet flow splits using backpressure. This
Axial-Flow Cyclone design achieves a broader range of separation effect than published
Reverse-Flow Cyclone designs. However, the unit will need to undergo further
development to reduce shear and maximise residence time at high swirl

evidence.title: Molecular pathways of silica nanoparticle formation and biosilicification
evidence.abstract:
Biosilicification and silica nanoparticle formation occur in many modem terrestrial environments and they also played an important role in ancient geological settings. This thesis presents results from (i) field studies in Icelandic geothermal waters that aimed at quantifying the parameters that control the growth rate and texture of sinters and the diversity and silicification of associated microbial communities and (ii) lab studies that focussed on the

kinetics and mechanisms of silica nanoparticle forination under conditions mimicking natural geothermal environments.



The analysis of growth rates and textures of sinters from five geochemically very different Icelandic geothermal areas showed that the inorganic silica precipitation rate was strongly influenced by temperature, pH, ionic strength, and silica concentration. In addition, the presence

of thick biofilms seemed to have aided the precipitation process by simply providing "sticky" surfaces. In turn, the structural and textural development of sinters was affected by the precipitation rate and mechanism (subaqueously and/or subaerially) as well as the presence and

absence of microbial communities. As a result, porous, subaequeouss inters developed at sites with medium to high sinter growth rates and low microbial activity. Conversely, dense, heterogeneouss inters formed in geothermal waters characterized by low precipitation rates and extensive biofilms. With time these biofilms became fully silicified and well preserved within the sinter edifices. The diversity of microbial communities in hot spring environments appeared to be directly controlled by the physico-chernical conditions of the geothermal waters (i. e., T,pH, salinity and sinter growth rate) and the most dominant phylotypes were related to Aquificae, Deinococci and y-Proteobacteria.



The rates and mechanisms of the initial steps of silica polymerisation and silica nanoparticle formation were quantified in-situ and time-resolved using synchrotron-based small angle x-ray scattering (SAXS). The experiments were carried out in near neutral pH solutions with initial

mechanism_map.mechanism: Coupled hydrothermal finite-element simulation of temperature and pressure fields can predict the hydrothermal conditions that drive mineral solubility, enabling operators to identify where flashed brine crosses into calcite/silica supersaturation and to shift operating conditions off the scaling envelope before deposition nucleates on internals.
mechanism_map.intervention: Build a calibrated reduced-order hydrothermal FE replica of the existing wellhead flash train and cyclone separators (clamp-on sensors and external modeling only, no pressure-boundary welding, geometry matched to the installed vessels), then use it to re-tune flash pressure, brine temperature drop, and injection-header flow paths so the brine's pressure-temperature trajectory stays below the calcite and silica gel saturation thresholds at the exact internal locations where scale currently forms.
mechanism_map.expected_effect: Deposition onset on separator internals and injection headers is pushed well beyond the current 45-60 day window, and the quarterly 6-11 percent thermal output loss shrinks as flow area and heat-transfer surface remain clean between maintenance cycles.
mechanism_map.falsification_test: Run the simulator against historical field data and check whether it reproduces the observed 45-60 day calcite onset and the downstream silica gel zoning; then implement the re-tuned flash conditions in a single pilot well and measure scale mass on removable coupons and separator pressure drop over two quarters, comparing against the eleven unchanged wells as control.

candidates.intervention: Install a bolted, adjustable internal weir (non-welded level-setting riser/downcomer) inside the existing wellhead cyclone separator to hold a controlled liquid inventory that keeps the barrel wall and internals wetted over the operating flow range, with no welding on the pressure boundary and dimensions fitted to the existing vessel geometry.

candidates.mechanism: Flashing is thermodynamically forced to supersaturate the brine with respect to calcite (CO2 degassing raises pH and strips carbonate buffering) and with respect to silica (cooling plus steam-phase concentration). Because that supersaturation cannot be avoided while still producing steam, the child consumes it instead: a sacrificial seeded contactor placed at the point of maximum supersaturation upstream of the cyclone supplies a very high density of preferred nucleation sites with tuned residence time, so calcite and polymerizing silica precipitate onto recoverable seed particles rather than nucleating heterogeneously on vessel walls and injection headers. Deposition on internals then requires adhesion work that the flowing shear and low-adhesion internal surfaces do not permit, and the dissolved-silica load carried to the injection header is reduced because a fraction of the silica is captured as solid seed coating upstream.
candidates.intervention: Retrofit a fluidized-bed seeded crystallizer as a bolted spool section in the brine line between the flash vessel and the cyclone separators (no pressure-boundary welding; matched flanges and existing supports), charged with calcite/silica seed media of controlled size, with seed withdrawal and make-up rate set from measured supersaturation. In parallel, give the cyclone internals and injection-header wetted surfaces a low-surface-energy electropolished or fluoropolymer/DLC-type finish so particles that do nucleate are swept through rather than bonded. Seed recirculation rate and bed inventory become a controlled operating variable, not a fixed design constant.
candidates.predicted_effect: Precipitation mass splits toward the seed bed: scale mass on removable coupons of separator internals falls by a large fraction relative to the 45-60 day baseline, separator pressure drop stays below 8 kPa across the full 90-day window, and injection-water dissolved silica is held below 120 ppm because silica is removed as solid seed coating upstream rather than gelling in the header. Quarterly thermal output loss of 6-11 percent shrinks as flow area and heat-transfer surface remain clean between maintenance cycles.
candidates.testable_prediction: Cheapest decisive test is a slipstream bench rig using actual field brine at measured flash conditions: run identical flash-and-settle sequences with and without the seed bed at the available residence time, then quantify (a) scale mass per unit area on witness coupons standing in for internals and (b) dissolved silica in the effluent. If the seed bed does not capture a clear majority of the precipitated calcite and does not measurably lower dissolved silica toward the 120 ppm target within the real residence-time budget, the child is killed before any full-scale retrofit.
candidates.mechanism_source_span: hydrothermal finite element (FE) simulator that can simulate the subsurface and its hydrothermal conditions
candidates.support_state_note: IMPROVE_CHILD_SUPPORT_NOT_ADJUDICATED: the child's mutated mechanism has no mechanism-space evidence adjudication; the release gate holds non-affirmative support states (R401 Phase 4)

derivation_trace.causal_change: The parent tried to keep the brine's pressure-temperature trajectory below calcite and silica saturation thresholds, which is infeasible because flashing itself creates the supersaturation; the child accepts unavoidable supersaturation and relocates where it is consumed, adding an upstream sacrificial nucleation sink so precipitation happens on recoverable seeds instead of on separator internals and headers. This directly answers the recorded failure mechanism by converting an impossible suppression strategy into a feasible site-control strategy.
derivation_trace.novel_design_variable: Upstream nucleation-site density, expressed as seed-bed inventory and seed recirculation/make-up rate per unit brine flow, which sets where precipitation mass deposits; the parent only varied flash pressure, brine temperature drop, and header flow paths.

CROSS_DOMAIN_MIN_NONGENERIC_OVERLAP.justification: R377 patent-text ground truth (TOSCANINI/R377_PATENT_TEXT_FETCH.json + R377_PATENT_TEXT_GROUND_TRUTH.json): 12/30 family representatives (40%) were substantively irrelevant cross-domain term collisions (CWDM optical link for a battery-thermal candidate; dental-condition monitoring for rolling stock; bone fracture forceps for rail steel...). A hit sharing NO entity term with the candidate now needs >= 3 NON-generic mechanism terms to be mechanism art: the measured true cross-domain analog (line-pipe steel with hydrogen fracture toughness for a rail-steel candidate) shares 3 non-generic terms and survives; every measured false positive shares <= 2 and is demoted. This RAISES the cross-domain bar (was the same >= 2 as same-domain) — stricter, not weaker (Art. VII).
CROSS_DOMAIN_MIN_NONGENERIC_OVERLAP.uncertainty: term overlap remains a proxy; entity word-sense collisions ('gear': steering vs draft) can still pass — disclosed limitation, not a solved problem

MIN_MECHANISM_OVERLAP.justification: same term-overlap rule family as the pipeline relevance adjudicator and the Q2 instrument (>= 2 shared content terms = domain-specific rather than accidental collision); NOT weakened relative to any prior gate
MIN_MECHANISM_OVERLAP.uncertainty: term overlap is a proxy for mechanism identity

ANTICIPATION_COVERAGE_RATIO.justification: a family ANTICIPATES only when nearly ALL elements of the candidate's FULL distinguishing set (uncapped — the claim elements, not the 6-term query core) appear in the family's claim/abstract text; 0.8 leaves a >= 20% element margin — anything lower would convert partial art into a kill (Art. XXVIII forbids). Measured adversarial case: a domain-only patent reached 0.857 against a capped denominator whose true differentiators (acoustic, multi-modal) had been ranked out
ANTICIPATION_COVERAGE_RATIO.uncertainty: claim coverage measured by term overlap, not a claim chart; recorded per family with evidence tier

MAX_QUERY_TERMS.justification: provider-measured sweet spot for keyword patent queries (longer queries dilute ranking)

hard_blocks.physical_constraint: CSF turnover rate = 2.88x/day = 259 turnovers in 90 days. No membrane or affinity mechanism can overcome this. The ceiling is PHYSIOLOGICAL (CSF production rate is a constant).
hard_blocks.lesson: Before investing in any retention mechanism, check the CSF TURNOVER RATE. The turnover rate (2.88x/day) is a physiological constant that makes long-term retention physically impossible for any membrane-based mechanism.
hard_blocks.domain_terms_source: entry vocabulary: physical_constraint + reusable_lesson + mechanism_name (stopword-normalized; generic epistemic words removed)

warnings.mechanism: R2-C3 predictor v1 — pressure-trajectory + phenotype classification for VSS failure-type prediction
warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM (sharpened per CEO Round 56o): 'Existing information + existing transformation + existing control, merely recombined, is insufficient. A combination qualifies only if it produces a demonstrably new technical effect that survives prior art and non-obviousness attack. A world-class invention needs a genuinely new technical information source, transformation, or control capability. Do not build an AI layer on top of an already-claimed sensing/control architecture.' NOTE: This theorem does NOT create a universal 'new sensor required' rule. A novel combination of existing measurements CAN qualify if it produces a new, technically non-obvious effect. The theorem rejects TRIVIAL recombination, not all combinations.

warnings.mechanism: OSV-4: HRV/autonomic state as orthogonal predictor for R2-C3
warnings.lesson: A signal can be GENUINELY ORTHOGONAL to a specific measurement architecture (Hakim measures pressure, not HRV) and still be a DOWNSTREAM CONSEQUENCE of the same physiological variable (ICP → sympathetic → HRV). Orthogonality to one architecture does not imply independence from the underlying physiology. Before claiming a signal is 'new information,' test whether it is causally downstream of an already-measured variable. If A → B and A is measured, then B is a proxy for A, not new information — even if B is measured by a different sensor.

Patent searches must generate terminology from patent claims + descriptions + CPC classes + inventor vocabulary + adjacent technologies, not just internally coined phrases. A query-fragile search produces false negatives.' The machine must be better at discovering what competitors actually claimed than it is at inventing elegant names for what we hope is new.

warnings.mechanism: Stroke: clot-vessel adhesion isolation + measurement + strategy selection (Layer A: force-decomposition estimator v1)
warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-016 (sharpened per CEO Round 58): A proposed latent quantity survives only when (1) identifiability is demonstrated under an EXPLICIT observation/dynamics model with full rank/observability analysis (not naive unknown-count), AND (2) identifiability REMAINS under plausible model uncertainty (each ideal assumption relaxed toward realistic physics and re-tested). A single favorable rank calculation under a convenient model is INSUFFICIENT. A single unfavorable perturbation model is ALSO INSUFFICIENT to claim universal non-identifiability — it only kills the specific estimator tested under that specific perturbation model. The correct procedure: (a) define state, observables, inputs, noise, known/unknown params; (b) build measurement equations; (c) test rank of Jacobian wrt unknown params; (d) perform adversarial model-uncertainty test: relax each assumption toward realistic physics and re-test identifiability under the combined relaxed model; (e) only if BOTH the ideal-model rank AND the adversarial-model rank hold (or constructively fail) can a universal claim (measurable OR non-measurable) be recorded.
warnings.action_required: Explicit justification required to proceed despite this constraint

warnings.territory: Cross-cutting (extracted from Stroke Round 58; applies to all latent-variable inventions)
warnings.mechanism: Structural identifiability under a convenient model is not enough — adversarial model-uncertainty and practical-operation survival are mandatory
warnings.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-017: A discovery engine earns trust when it attacks its own successful proof harder than its unsuccessful ideas. Structural identifiability under a convenient model is not enough. A candidate must survive adversarial model uncertainty AND practical operation (safety, timing, decision value, first-pass vs post-hoc). The burden is bidirectional: (a) the proposer must demonstrate identifiability survives realistic model relaxation; (b) the killer must demonstrate non-identifiability holds under EVERY plausible estimator and measurement protocol, not just the one they chose to attack. When in doubt, the implementation is killed; the scientific question stays open until either (a) a survivor is found or (b) an explicit non-identifiability counterexample is constructed (two physically distinct latent states producing indistinguishable observations under ALL measurement protocols).
warnings.action_required: Explicit justification required to proceed despite this constraint

warnings.territory: Cross-cutting (extracted from Round 62 capability collision failure; applies to ALL novelty claims)
warnings.mechanism: Capability collision test — keyword collision search is insufficient to establish novelty
warnings.lesson:
FROZEN THEOREM CE-018: A novelty claim survives only when the candidate's CAPABILITY (what it can DO) is demonstrably absent from the prior art landscape — not when the candidate's KEYWORDS (what words it uses) are absent. The correct procedure: (1) decompose the candidate into its functional capabilities (e.g., 'intrapprocedural clot sensing' not 'retrieved-clot physical signature measurement'); (2) search the prior art landscape for each capability using the prior art's own vocabulary (assignee names, CPC classes, commercial product names, inventor terminology); (3) build a capability collision matrix mapping each capability to prior art coverage; (4) only if at least one capability is genuinely UNOCCUPIED (confirmed by both patent search AND commercial frontier analysis) can a novelty claim be recorded. Semantic re-skins (CE-012 violation) include: 'retrieved-clot' vs 'in-situ clot'; 'physical signature' vs 'composition'; 'integrated sensor' vs 'catheter-mounted sensor.' These distinctions prove nothing. The test is capability, not vocabulary.

SHARPENED (per CEO Round 62 audit): Capability novelty must be evaluated at the FUNCTIONAL END-TO-END level: input → inference → decision → physical effect → measurable outcome. Otherwise the machine can still find a 'novel' intermediate layer (e.g., a new sensor modality, a new feature, a new algorithm) that is already covered by an existing end-to-end system. The correct end-to-end test: (5) decompose the candidate into the complete causal loop — what is observed → what is inferred → what is predicted → what physical action becomes possible → what measurable outcome changes; (6) map each step of this loop to the prior art's end-to-end systems (not just individual capabilities); (7) only if the candidate's complete causal loop is demonstrably absent from the prior art's end-to-end systems can a novelty claim be recorded. A 'novel' intermediate layer that plugs into an existing end-to-end system is NOT novel — it is a substitution, not an invention. The unit of novelty is the complete causal loop, not the sensor, feature, algorithm, or capability.

informational.mechanism: M3_REFINED electrothermal SMA retrieval
informational.lesson: ALWAYS report worst-case reliability for clinical devices. Averages mask catastrophic failure modes. Thermal activation in a 37°C body environment has a narrow window (37-45°C = 8°C max). Sensor electronics are a SPOF that cannot be fully resolved by redundancy (common-mode failures).

informational.mechanism: M5_REFINED adaptive over-drainage controller (sleep-state + venous pressure)
informational.lesson: Do not assume VP shunt problems apply to the eShunt. The eShunt's drainage geometry is fundamentally different (short path, no siphon). Always verify the problem exists for the SPECIFIC device geometry. Over-drainage is siphon-driven; without a hydrostatic column, it may not occur.

informational.mechanism: Flow reversal obstruction clearing (R3)
informational.lesson: Retrograde flush for eShunt pushes debris toward brain. The eShunt venous drainage direction makes retrograde more dangerous than VP shunts (peritoneal). However, the clinical hazard is ANALOGICAL (SAH blood causes inflammation), not directly proven for shunt debris. MODEL_DERIVED + ANALOGICAL_EVIDENCE — not PROVEN_UNSAFE.

informational.mechanism: RES-4 narrow: adaptive transverse/sigmoid sinus stent for CSF absorption regulation via AG pressure gradient control
informational.lesson: MODEL-BOUNDED NEGATIVE RESULT: Before inventing variable geometry, calculate absolute pressure-control authority at the actual operating point. Relative r^4 sensitivity is meaningless if the absolute pressure drop is tiny. Under realistic post-stenting conditions (D=5-10mm, Q=200-500 mL/min), adaptive diameter control of a venous sinus produces <0.2 mmHg change in AG gradient — 5x below the 1 mmHg pre-registered threshold. Control authority exists only in the stenotic+high-flow regime (D≤4mm, Q≥1200 mL/min), which is incompatible with a stented patient whose stent has normalized diameter to 7-10mm. The network model (1323 configs) confirms: flow redistribution through contralateral sinus does NOT rescue control authority (dominance has no effect). NOT a universal vascular invariant — based on Poiseuille model with specific assumptions about geometry, flow, and topology.

informational.mechanism: Minimum Sufficient Validation Evidence Derivation (MSVED) — 4-link chain: ML change → clinical pathway → risk envelope → minimum sufficient evidence → sufficiency proof
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-019: A clinical-pathway-aware evidence selector must demonstrate that the clinical-pathway bridge produces a MATERIALLY DIFFERENT and BETTER evidence set than information-maximizing selection (BOED). If the pathway-aware selector uses MORE tests while achieving WORSE assurance, the clinical-pathway bridge adds complexity without value. The minimum-evidence claim must be validated by showing tests_required < BOED, not just tests_required < conventional. The killer experiment must compare against the STRONGEST available baseline (BOED), not just conventional full-validation.

informational.mechanism: Automated Sufficiency Proof Generator (CC-04 / MSES theorem) — formal proof that a specific evidence set E is sufficient to establish modification-specific clinical risk envelope R(Δ)
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-020: A sufficiency proof that is merely an integration of known statistical methods (NI testing + coverage + multiple-testing correction + sensitivity analysis) is NOT a novel mathematical result. Under §103, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is likely obvious (KSR v. Teleflex). The frontier is a NEW MATHEMATICAL BOUND — e.g., a tight bound on minimum evidence set size that is better than what existing methods give individually, or a proof technique that connects clinical pathway coverage to statistical sufficiency in a way that is not derivable from existing theory. Additionally: killer tests for sufficiency proofs must include a TRUE POSITIVE case (sufficient evidence for a SAFE modification that the system correctly accepts), not just a true negative (insufficient evidence that the system correctly rejects).

informational.mechanism: Non-Inferiority Statistical Engine (CC-08) — automated paired NI comparison with pre-registered margins for ML model modifications
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-021: Automating a standard statistical test (NI testing) for a regulatory context that explicitly requires it (PCCP) is NOT an invention. Under KSR, combining known methods to solve a problem the market explicitly asks for is obvious. The coder correctly identified this in the R254 ranking ("NI testing is standard, high collision risk") but incorrectly chose to proceed. The CEO corrected: high collision risk is a RED FLAG, not a reason to proceed. Kill immediately if the smallest surviving mechanism is standard statistics + ML context + automated reporting.

informational.mechanism: SGET (Strain-Gated Electrochemical Transduction) — A=strain pulse changes B=electrochemical sensor from 2D surface to 3D depth profiling. First synergy-2 candidate.
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-022: Synergy ≠ novelty and synergy ≠ commercial moat. A functional interaction (A changes B) is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT for invention. The interaction itself — the causal law, the emergent effect, and functional equivalents across domains — must survive prior art independently. Additionally: synergy claims without quantitative comparison against the STRONGEST baseline are stories, not evidence. The unexpected-effect proof requires: (1) pre-registered quantitative prediction, (2) strongest baseline identified, (3) killer experiment vs that baseline, (4) result not predictable from A and B independently. The new standard: A changes B → unexpected effect → interaction survives prior art → reproducible advantage → cannot be cheaply reproduced → buyer value.

informational.mechanism: SC-05 Biofilm-Resistant Living-Surface Venous Interface — continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface with active surface-energy control at CSF-blood interface
informational.lesson: FROZEN THEOREM CE-023: A candidate that survives the 14-gate protocol at the CONCEPT level can be killed at the ELEMENT-DECOMPOSITION level. The 14 gates assessed M4 against the broad concept (continuously renewing anti-biofilm surface) and found M4=NOT FOUND. But deep collision revealed that each element (continuous renewal, dynamic topography, surface-energy modulation) is individually occupied by prior art. The combination is an aggregation of known anti-fouling approaches. The lesson: M4 must be assessed at the ELEMENT level, not the concept level. And M4=NOT FOUND means the search has not found comparable performance yet — not that it does not exist.

custody_records.raw_content: Geothermal heat, as renewable energy, shows great advantage with respect to its environmental impact due to its significantly lower CO2 emissions than conventional fossil fuel. Open and closed-loop geothermal heat pumps, which utilize shallow geothermal systems, are an efficient technology for cooling and heating buildings, especially in urban areas. Integrated use of geothermal energy technologies for district heating, cooling, and thermal energy storage can be applied to optimize the subsurface for communities to provide them with multiple sustainable energy and community resilience benefits. The utilization of the subsurface resources may lead to a variation in the underground environment, which might further impact local environmental conditions. However, very few simulators can handle such a highly complex set of coupled computations on a regional or city scale. We have developed high-performance computing (HPC) based hydrothermal finite element (FE) simulator that can simulate the subsurface and its hydrothermal conditions at a scale of tens of km. The HPC simulator enables us to investigate the subsurface thermal and hydrologic response to the built underground environment (such as basements and subways) at the community scale. In this study, a coupled hydrothermal simulator is developed based on the open-source finite element library deal.II. The HPC simulator was validated by comparing the results of a benchmark case study against COMSOL Multiphysics, in which Aquifer Thermal Energy Storage (ATES) is modeled and a process of heat injection into ATES is simulated. The use of an energy pile system at the Treasure Island redevelopment site (San Francisco, CA, USA) was selected as a case study to demonstrate the HPC capability of the developed simulator. The simulator is capable of modeling multiple city-scale geothermal scenarios in a reasonable amount of time.

custody_records.raw_content: Closed-loop shallow geothermal systems are one of the key technologies for decarbonizing the residential heating and cooling sector. The primary type of these systems involves vertical borehole heat exchangers (BHEs). During the planning phase, it is essential to find the optimal design for these systems, including the depth and spatial arrangement of the BHEs. In this work, we have developed a novel approach to find the optimal design of BHE fields, taking into account constraints such as temperature limits of the heat carrier fluid. These limits correspond to the regulatory practices applied during the planning phase. The approach uses a finite line source model to simulate temperature changes in the ground in combination with an analytical model of heat transport within the boreholes. Our approach is demonstrated using realistic scenarios and is expected to improve current practice in the planning and design of BHE systems.

custody_records.raw_content: Treedepth decomposition has several practical applications and can be used to speed up many parameterized algorithms. There are several works aiming to design a scalable algorithm to compute exact treedepth decompositions. Those include works based on a set of all minimal separators. In those algorithms, although a number of minimal separators are enumerated, the minimal separators that are used for an optimal solution are empirically very small. Therefore, analyzing the upper bound on the size of minimal separators is an important problem because it has the potential to significantly reduce the computation time. A minimal separator $S$ is called an optimal top separator if $td(G) = |S| + td(G \backslash S)$, where $td(G)$ denotes the treedepth of $G$. Then, we have two theoretical results on the size of optimal top separators. (1) For any $G$, there is an optimal top separator $S$ such that $|S| \le 2tw(G)$, where $tw(G)$ is the treewidth of $G$. (2) For any $c < 2$, there exists a graph $G$ such that any optimal top separator $S$ of $G$ have $|S| > c \cdot tw(G)$, i.e., the first result gives a tight bound on the size of an optimal top separator.

Conventional bulk oil-water separation is performed in large gravity separators that take
up large areas and potentially contain large volumes of hazardous material. An
intensified bulk separator has the potential to provide significant benefit in saving space,
especially where this is at a premium, and in improving safety.
The I-SEP, a novel geometry of Axial-Flow Cyclone (also known as Uniflow or
straight-through) separator, has been tested as an intensified bulk oil-water separator.
The objective of this work is to quantify performance by producing a map of separation
performance with variation of inlet conditions, using variation of outlet back pressure to
make the separator adaptable to variable inlet flow. A second objective is to compare
the experimental performance of the I-SEP with a mathematical model.
Using a Perspex test-unit with kerosene, or a silicone-based oil, and water in a batch
flow loop, a map has been produced for outlet compositions and separation efficiencies
at multiple inlet velocities. This was done for a range of inlet water cuts from 10% to
90% and with a geometry varied by lengthening the separating chamber of the test unit.
A Computational Fluid Dynamics model using the Reynolds-Stress model has been
developed with the FLUENT 6.0 CFD code. This has been compared with quantitative
flow visualisation data and drop sizing information to model the separation of the
cyclone by a discrete-phase technique.
An optimum configuration and operating conditions has been found, with peak
efficiencies in excess of 80%. This shows the important effect in improving
performance achieved by the manipulation of outlet flow splits using backpressure. This
Axial-Flow Cyclone design achieves a broader range of separation effect than published
Reverse-Flow Cyclone designs. However, the unit will need to undergo further
development to reduce shear and maximise residence time at high swirl

Biosilicification and silica nanoparticle formation occur in many modem terrestrial environments and they also played an important role in ancient geological settings. This thesis presents results from (i) field studies in Icelandic geothermal waters that aimed at quantifying the parameters that control the growth rate and texture of sinters and the diversity and silicification of associated microbial communities and (ii) lab studies that focussed on the

kinetics and mechanisms of silica nanoparticle forination under conditions mimicking natural geothermal environments.



The analysis of growth rates and textures of sinters from five geochemically very different Icelandic geothermal areas showed that the inorganic silica precipitation rate was strongly influenced by temperature, pH, ionic strength, and silica concentration. In addition, the presence

of thick biofilms seemed to have aided the precipitation process by simply providing "sticky" surfaces. In turn, the structural and textural development of sinters was affected by the precipitation rate and mechanism (subaqueously and/or subaerially) as well as the presence and

absence of microbial communities. As a result, porous, subaequeouss inters developed at sites with medium to high sinter growth rates and low microbial activity. Conversely, dense, heterogeneouss inters formed in geothermal waters characterized by low precipitation rates and extensive biofilms. With time these biofilms became fully silicified and well preserved within the sinter edifices. The diversity of microbial communities in hot spring environments appeared to be directly controlled by the physico-chernical conditions of the geothermal waters (i. e., T,pH, salinity and sinter growth rate) and the most dominant phylotypes were related to Aquificae, Deinococci and y-Proteobacteria.



The rates and mechanisms of the initial steps of silica polymerisation and silica nanoparticle formation were quantified in-situ and time-resolved using synchrotron-based small angle x-ray scattering (SAXS). The experiments were carried out in near neutral pH solutions with initial

value.mechanism: Flashing is thermodynamically forced to supersaturate the brine with respect to calcite (CO2 degassing raises pH and strips carbonate buffering) and with respect to silica (cooling plus steam-phase concentration). Because that supersaturation cannot be avoided while still producing steam, the child consumes it instead: a sacrificial seeded contactor placed at the point of maximum supersaturation upstream of the cyclone supplies a very high density of preferred nucleation sites with tuned residence time, so calcite and polymerizing silica precipitate onto recoverable seed particles rather than nucleating heterogeneously on vessel walls and injection headers. Deposition on internals then requires adhesion work that the flowing shear and low-adhesion internal surfaces do not permit, and the dissolved-silica load carried to the injection header is reduced because a fraction of the silica is captured as solid seed coating upstream.
value.intervention: Retrofit a fluidized-bed seeded crystallizer as a bolted spool section in the brine line between the flash vessel and the cyclone separators (no pressure-boundary welding; matched flanges and existing supports), charged with calcite/silica seed media of controlled size, with seed withdrawal and make-up rate set from measured supersaturation. In parallel, give the cyclone internals and injection-header wetted surfaces a low-surface-energy electropolished or fluoropolymer/DLC-type finish so particles that do nucleate are swept through rather than bonded. Seed recirculation rate and bed inventory become a controlled operating variable, not a fixed design constant.

doi:10.48550/arxiv.2103.00081.title: An HPC-Based Hydrothermal Finite Element Simulator for Modeling Underground Response to Community-Scale Geothermal Energy Production
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2103.00081.abstract: Geothermal heat, as renewable energy, shows great advantage with respect to its environmental impact due to its significantly lower CO2 emissions than conventional fossil fuel. Open and closed-loop geothermal heat pumps, which utilize shallow geothermal systems, are an efficient technology for cooling and heating buildings, especially in urban areas. Integrated use of geothermal energy technologies for district heating, cooling, and thermal energy storage can be applied to optimize the subsurface for communities to provide them with multiple sustainable energy and community resilience benefits. The utilization of the subsurface resources may lead to a variation in the underground environment, which might further impact local environmental conditions. However, very few simulators can handle such a highly complex set of coupled computations on a regional or city scale. We have developed high-performance computing (HPC) based hydrothermal finite element (FE) simulator that can simulate the subsurface and its hydrothermal conditions at a scale of tens of km. The HPC simulator enables us to investigate the subsurface thermal and hydrologic response to the built underground environment (such as basements and subways) at the community scale. In this study, a coupled hydrothermal simulator is developed based on the open-source finite element library deal.II. The HPC simulator was validated by comparing the results of a benchmark case study against COMSOL Multiphysics, in which Aquifer Thermal Energy Storage (ATES) is modeled and a process of heat injection into ATES is simulated. The use of an energy pile system at the Treasure Island redevelopment site (San Francisco, CA, USA) was selected as a case study to demonstrate the HPC capability of the developed simulator. The simulator is capable of modeling multiple city-scale geothermal scenarios in a reasonable amount of time.

doi:10.48550/arxiv.2603.24957.title: Optimization of Closed-Loop Shallow Geothermal Systems Using Analytical Models
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2603.24957.abstract: Closed-loop shallow geothermal systems are one of the key technologies for decarbonizing the residential heating and cooling sector. The primary type of these systems involves vertical borehole heat exchangers (BHEs). During the planning phase, it is essential to find the optimal design for these systems, including the depth and spatial arrangement of the BHEs. In this work, we have developed a novel approach to find the optimal design of BHE fields, taking into account constraints such as temperature limits of the heat carrier fluid. These limits correspond to the regulatory practices applied during the planning phase. The approach uses a finite line source model to simulate temperature changes in the ground in combination with an analytical model of heat transport within the boreholes. Our approach is demonstrated using realistic scenarios and is expected to improve current practice in the planning and design of BHE systems.

doi:10.48550/arxiv.2008.09822.title: On the Size of Minimal Separators for Treedepth Decomposition
doi:10.48550/arxiv.2008.09822.abstract: Treedepth decomposition has several practical applications and can be used to speed up many parameterized algorithms. There are several works aiming to design a scalable algorithm to compute exact treedepth decompositions. Those include works based on a set of all minimal separators. In those algorithms, although a number of minimal separators are enumerated, the minimal separators that are used for an optimal solution are empirically very small. Therefore, analyzing the upper bound on the size of minimal separators is an important problem because it has the potential to significantly reduce the computation time. A minimal separator $S$ is called an optimal top separator if $td(G) = |S| + td(G \backslash S)$, where $td(G)$ denotes the treedepth of $G$. Then, we have two theoretical results on the size of optimal top separators. (1) For any $G$, there is an optimal top separator $S$ such that $|S| \le 2tw(G)$, where $tw(G)$ is the treewidth of $G$. (2) For any $c < 2$, there exists a graph $G$ such that any optimal top separator $S$ of $G$ have $|S| > c \cdot tw(G)$, i.e., the first result gives a tight bound on the size of an optimal top separator.

title:1820dfd53870b635.title: Oil/water separation in a novel cyclone separator
title:1820dfd53870b635.abstract:
Conventional bulk oil-water separation is performed in large gravity separators that take
up large areas and potentially contain large volumes of hazardous material. An
intensified bulk separator has the potential to provide significant benefit in saving space,
especially where this is at a premium, and in improving safety.
The I-SEP, a novel geometry of Axial-Flow Cyclone (also known as Uniflow or
straight-through) separator, has been tested as an intensified bulk oil-water separator.
The objective of this work is to quantify performance by producing a map of separation
performance with variation of inlet conditions, using variation of outlet back pressure to
make the separator adaptable to variable inlet flow. A second objective is to compare
the experimental performance of the I-SEP with a mathematical model.
Using a Perspex test-unit with kerosene, or a silicone-based oil, and water in a batch
flow loop, a map has been produced for outlet compositions and separation efficiencies
at multiple inlet velocities. This was done for a range of inlet water cuts from 10% to
90% and with a geometry varied by lengthening the separating chamber of the test unit.
A Computational Fluid Dynamics model using the Reynolds-Stress model has been
developed with the FLUENT 6.0 CFD code. This has been compared with quantitative
flow visualisation data and drop sizing information to model the separation of the
cyclone by a discrete-phase technique.
An optimum configuration and operating conditions has been found, with peak
efficiencies in excess of 80%. This shows the important effect in improving
performance achieved by the manipulation of outlet flow splits using backpressure. This
Axial-Flow Cyclone design achieves a broader range of separation effect than published
Reverse-Flow Cyclone designs. However, the unit will need to undergo further
development to reduce shear and maximise residence time at high swirl

title:47fe720988863d05.title: Molecular pathways of silica nanoparticle formation and biosilicification
title:47fe720988863d05.abstract:
Biosilicification and silica nanoparticle formation occur in many modem terrestrial environments and they also played an important role in ancient geological settings. This thesis presents results from (i) field studies in Icelandic geothermal waters that aimed at quantifying the parameters that control the growth rate and texture of sinters and the diversity and silicification of associated microbial communities and (ii) lab studies that focussed on the

kinetics and mechanisms of silica nanoparticle forination under conditions mimicking natural geothermal environments.



The analysis of growth rates and textures of sinters from five geochemically very different Icelandic geothermal areas showed that the inorganic silica precipitation rate was strongly influenced by temperature, pH, ionic strength, and silica concentration. In addition, the presence

of thick biofilms seemed to have aided the precipitation process by simply providing "sticky" surfaces. In turn, the structural and textural development of sinters was affected by the precipitation rate and mechanism (subaqueously and/or subaerially) as well as the presence and

absence of microbial communities. As a result, porous, subaequeouss inters developed at sites with medium to high sinter growth rates and low microbial activity. Conversely, dense, heterogeneouss inters formed in geothermal waters characterized by low precipitation rates and extensive biofilms. With time these biofilms became fully silicified and well preserved within the sinter edifices. The diversity of microbial communities in hot spring environments appeared to be directly controlled by the physico-chernical conditions of the geothermal waters (i. e., T,pH, salinity and sinter growth rate) and the most dominant phylotypes were related to Aquificae, Deinococci and y-Proteobacteria.



The rates and mechanisms of the initial steps of silica polymerisation and silica nanoparticle formation were quantified in-situ and time-resolved using synchrotron-based small angle x-ray scattering (SAXS). The experiments were carried out in near neutral pH solutions with initial

system_architecture.description: PROPOSED architecture (no physical system exists): heat source characterization; conduction path / spreader; reject interface; safety limit interlock — realizing: Retrofit a fluidized-bed seeded crystallizer as a bolted spool section in the brine line between the flash vessel and the cyclone separators (no pressure-boundary welding; matched flanges and existing supports), charged with calcite/silica seed media of controlled size, with seed withdrawal and make-up rate set from measured supersaturation. In parallel, give the cyclone internals and injection-header wetted surfaces a low-surface-energy electropolished or fluoropolymer/DLC-type finish so particles that do nucleate are swept through rather than bonded. Seed recirculation rate and bed inventory become a controlled operating variable, not a fixed design constant.

design_inputs.value: no welding on the pressure boundary, fits existing vessel geometry

Flashing is thermodynamically forced to supersaturate the brine with respect to calcite (CO2 degassing raises pH and strips carbonate buffering) and with respect to silica (cooling plus steam-phase concentration). Because that supersaturation cannot be avoided while still producing steam, the child consumes it instead: a sacrificial seeded contactor placed at the point of maximum supersaturation upstream of the cyclone supplies a very high density of preferred nucleation sites with tuned residence time, so calcite and polymerizing silica precipitate onto recoverable seed particles rather than nucleating heterogeneously on vessel walls and injection headers. Deposition on internals then requires adhesion work that the flowing shear and low-adhesion internal surfaces do not permit, and the dissolved-silica load carried to the injection header is reduced because a fraction of the silica is captured as solid seed coating upstream.

proposed_design.input: no welding on the pressure boundary, fits existing vessel geometry
proposed_design.mechanism: Flashing is thermodynamically forced to supersaturate the brine with respect to calcite (CO2 degassing raises pH and strips carbonate buffering) and with respect to silica (cooling plus steam-phase concentration). Because that supersaturation cannot be avoided while still producing steam, the child consumes it instead: a sacrificial seeded contactor placed at the point of maximum supersaturation upstream of the cyclone supplies a very high density of preferred nucleation sites with tuned residence time, so calcite and polymerizing silica precipitate onto recoverable seed particles rather than nucleating heterogeneously on vessel walls and injection headers. Deposition on internals then requires adhesion work that the flowing shear and low-adhesion internal surfaces do not permit, and the dissolved-silica load carried to the injection header is reduced because a fraction of the silica is captured as solid seed coating upstream.
proposed_design.component_architecture: heat source characterization; conduction path / spreader; reject interface; safety limit interlock

heat source characterization realizing Retrofit a fluidized-bed seeded crystallizer as a bolted spool section in the brine line between the flash vessel and the cyclone separators (no pressure-boundary welding; matched flanges and existing supports), charged with calcite/silica seed media of controlled size, with seed withdrawal and make-up rate set from measured supersaturation. In parallel, give the cyclone internals and injection-header wetted surfaces a low-surface-energy electropolished or fluoropolymer/DLC-type finish so particles that do nucleate are swept through rather than bonded. Seed recirculation rate and bed inventory become a controlled operating variable, not a fixed design constant.
